ut_chaos_boulder.blurb: Chaos Boulder is the biggest block at Big Bend, a bouldering zone along the river north of Moab, and it holds a dozen problems. The grades spread from easy V1 up to a few very hard testpieces, with the middle of the range thin, so it suits strong boulderers more than beginners. The sandstone is delicate and the area has a stiff reputation for grading, so expect the lower numbers to feel firm. Landings are mostly friendly, there is no real approach, and the boulder is easy to spot by the chalk piled on its low holds. It is a good option once the cooler months arrive.

ut_gridwall.blurb: Gridwall is a limestone sport wall high on the north side of American Fork Canyon in the southern Wasatch, with a dozen bolted lines. The wall is gently overhanging and the climbing is hard: nearly everything falls in the 5.10 to 5.12 range, mostly 5.11 and 5.12, so it is not a place for warming up on easy grades. Because it sits up high and catches plenty of sun, it works as a winter crag on clear days, and a water bottle matters on warm ones. The hike in is steep and has a reputation for being tiring.

ut_hulk_the.blurb: The Hulk is a single sandstone boulder in the Right Fork of Joe's Valley, close to the dirt road that runs up past the old coal mine. It carries about a dozen problems, spread from V3 through a cluster at V5 and V6 and on up to a few hard test pieces from V8 to V10. There is hardly any walking involved, but little else sits within easy reach, so it makes a quick stop rather than a full day. The rock is porous and loses strength when damp, so give it a long dry spell before pulling on.

ut_orangutan_wall.blurb: Orangutan Wall is a sport crag on the Left Fork of Maple Canyon, with a dozen bolted routes on the cobbled conglomerate that defines the canyon. Most lines are moderate, running from 5.7 through 5.10, which makes it a friendly place for climbers building up to harder Maple routes. Routes are on the long side by canyon standards, and a 60 m rope is a sensible choice. The wall catches early shade and again later in the day, so it stays comfortable through much of the day, and the hike from the Left Fork trail is short.

ut_purple_wall.blurb: Purple Wall is the first crag you reach in the Maybird Slide Area of Little Cottonwood Canyon, with twelve bolted sport routes on steep, juggy quartz monzonite. Grades cluster around 5.10, with a few 5.9s and a single 5.11, so it works well for newer leaders and anyone wanting a pumpy tick list without hard moves. Bolts are generally clipped from good stances. The wall faces east and slips into shade by mid-afternoon, which suits hot summer days, and the quiet setting adds to the appeal. Some sections of rock are still a little loose.
ut_purple_wall.approach: Roughly 20 to 25 minutes on a cairned trail through a rock-filled gulch from the roadside pullout, passing the ruins of two stone huts near the wall.

ut_scar_the.blurb: The Scar is a steep sport cliff above Potash Road, looking out over Moab, the wetlands and the Colorado River. All twelve routes overhang, run roughly 30 to 70 feet, and pump you out on flat holds. Grades start at 5.11 and climb through 5.12 into the 5.13 range, so it is a venue for strong sport climbers. The sandstone here has more calcite than typical Moab rock and feels more solid. The wall gets morning sun and afternoon shade, often with a light breeze, which makes it a pleasant spot as days warm up.

ut_simpson_rock.blurb: Simpson Rock sits in the Right Fork of Maple Canyon, only a short walk up-canyon from the Right Fork parking area. It is mostly a sport crag with a dozen entries, including one easy boulder problem. The routes spread from 5.6 up through 5.10 and into 5.12, so there is something for beginners and a couple of hard projects for experts. The south and west faces overhang steeply while the east face is more vertical, and the northeast side tends to stay shady, handy for a warm-up on a hot day.

ut_sunday_wall.blurb: Sunday Wall is a quartzite trad sector in the middle of the Schoolroom, the tiered cliff band above Ogden. Walls are 50 to 80 feet, with moderate routes from about 5.4 into the 5.10 range, plus one top-rope line. Most lines go with a single rack of cams and nuts, though a few ask for small gear. Loose rock was cleaned during development, so the quality is generally good. It is a decent trad choice that avoids the traffic and loose rock of Ogden Canyon. The wall has morning shade and afternoon sun. Reaching it takes a steady uphill hike.
